findings.title: commit() called with one argument but arroyo's Commit requires two
findings.body: In `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, the inner `commit_offsets` closure calls `commit(commit_data)` with a single argument, but arroyo's `Commit` type is `Callable[[Mapping[Partition, int], bool], None]`. At runtime this raises `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'force'`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`. The result is that offsets are never committed, the offset tracker grows without bound, and on restart the consumer re-reads everything it has already processed (defeating the whole point of the commit loop and potentially causing data-integrity issues for non-idempotent result processors). The fix is `commit(commit_data, False)` (or wrap with `CommitOffsets`). The unit tests miss this because they pass a mock with a default for `force`.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps references undefined variables
findings.body: Inside `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` only `all_commits` and `test_partition` are defined, but the final assertion reads `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`. Neither `committed_offsets` nor `partition` exists in the test scope, so the test raises `NameError` before any assertion runs and provides no coverage of the gap-fill behavior it claims to test. The assertion should use `all_commits[-1][test_partition]` (or similar) so it actually exercises the production code path.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps asserts wrong offset value
findings.body: After filling the gap by submitting offset 101, all of offsets 100-103 are processed, so `get_committable_offsets` returns `{test_partition: 103}`. `commit_offsets` then adds +1 (it explicitly comments "the committed offset should represent the next offset to read from") and calls `commit({test_partition: 104})`. The test asserts `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`, but the actual value should be 104. This is inconsistent with the first assertion in the same test (`actual_offset == 101` for processing up to 100) which correctly accounts for the +1.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts opposite of expected behavior
findings.body: The test docstring claims "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires that no commits happen at all (or that the partition is absent). In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, exceptions from `result_processor` are caught by `except Exception` and the offset is still marked complete in the `finally` block, so the commit loop will eventually emit `{test_partition: 102}` for the two submitted messages. The assertion will fail and the test passes only when the implementation does the opposite of what the test name claims. The assertion should instead verify that `test_partition` is present and committed to 102.

findings.title: get_queue_for_group uses Python's hash(), not consistent hashing
findings.body: `get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` and its docstring says "consistent hashing". Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized across processes (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same `group_key` can be assigned to a different queue on every restart. Within a single process lifetime ordering is preserved (which is what the consumer relies on, since in-flight items are lost on restart anyway), but the function does not provide the cross-process stability the docstring advertises, and it isn't true consistent hashing (e.g. it doesn't survive changes in `num_queues`). Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32` and either drop the "consistent" wording or use a hash ring.

findings.title: --mode help text does not describe thread-queue-parallel
findings.body: `uptime_options` adds `"thread-queue-parallel"` to the choice list, but the `help` text still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." with no mention of the new mode or how its parallelism differs (queue-based, per-group ordering, etc.). Operators picking the mode have no way to know what the new option does or how it differs from the existing parallel modes.

findings.title: Queue depth metric is not tagged by worker/queue
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` only with `tags={"identifier": self.identifier}`. With `num_queues=20` workers sharing the same identifier, all depth values are aggregated into one series and individual hot queues cannot be distinguished, defeating the purpose of the metric for diagnosing the very backlog problem the PR is meant to address. The worker_id (and ideally the queue index) should be in the tags.

findings.title: wait_until_empty is dead code
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty` is defined but never called by the strategy or factory. It also has subtle correctness issues if ever used (it polls `qsize()` rather than tracking completion, so it can race against in-flight items). Either remove it or document and test its intended use.
